description: I’m a second-year Aerospace Engineering student at Loughborough University, building a game where players don’t just fly a spacecraft, they design one for a specific mission.
summary: ASTRONI is a browser game about planning and flying a real space mission. A science satellite, AURORA-7, has been hit by space debris, and the player's small space company must save it within 72 hours on a $250M budget. Players design a rocket from parts using real physics (rocket equation, staging, orbital transfers), launch it, and handle one random event based on real NASA data, such as a solar flare from NASA's DONKI records. Then they inspect the damage with a robotic arm, repair the satellite on a spacewalk and bring the crew home. Every design choice changes what happens in space, and the mission report explains in plain English, with numbers, why the mission succeeded or failed, so students learn real space science by playing.
details:
Detailed Project Description:

ASTRONI is a browser game for secondary-school physics students. It answers the Space Mission Design Game challenge: define a mission, design the spacecraft, manage resources, simulate the mission and learn from the result.

What it does: Players get a contract to save AURORA-7, a fictional Earth-observation satellite whose solar array was destroyed by space debris. They have 72 hours and a $250M budget.

How it works:

  1. Workshop: build a staged rocket in 3D from casings, fuel tanks, engines, decouplers, boosters, fins, a capsule and a cargo module. Live readouts show cost, mass, thrust-to-weight, Δv per stage and a mission Δv bar, with a checklist (heat shield, parachutes, RCS, cargo packed).
  2. Approach choice: standard transfer, fast intercept (more fuel) or patient phasing (more time).
  3. Launch: your own stages separate as designed. The flight is simulated leg by leg with the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, using the ship's real mass at each burn.
  4. Random event: one per run, from engine out, a solar flare (replaying real NASA DONKI flare records), a debris warning and a fuel leak, plus a comms blackout. Batteries, debris shields, antennas and extra engines reduce their effects.
  5. Robotic arm: steer the arm (live inverse kinematics) to inspect the satellite with a wrist camera, find hidden damage, and move the new solar panel across.
  6. Spacewalk: first-person repair with oxygen and a tether: unbolt, fit, splice the cable, patch the radiator, retrieve the data module.
  7. System test and return: check power, temperature and data, then de-orbit, re-enter and land. A missing heat shield or parachutes means failure.
  8. Mission report: grade, score breakdown, and plain-English causes with numbers. "Fly again" replays the same random events.

Benefits: students learn why rockets need stages, how fuel and mass trade off, and how one design decision affects a whole mission, using real NASA data.

Built with: Three.js, Vite and JavaScript, with 25 automated physics tests; hosted on Vercel. All 3D models were made by the team in Fusion 360.

Next: Missions 2–3 (lunar cargo, debris cleanup) and co-op roles.
